summary:
Ñuble is a region of Chile, and visitors enter and are treated under Chile's national framework. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults change registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry with no therapy or surgery requirement, applicants aged 14 to 18 apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute's under-14 wording was declared inapplicable as unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court on 9 April 2025 in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, with the ruling confined to that case.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum; Article 10 allows complementary protection to recognised asylum seekers, and no foreigner holding it may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022 and civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Detention carries specific rules. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Transphobic violence remains documented. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, with an acquaintance perpetrator who confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Ñuble recorded the sharpest regional increase in documented homo/transphobic abuse in the country during 2024, rising 300% from a 1.44% share of the national total. Formal trans legal presence in the region remains thin: 12,669 people have changed legal name and sex nationally since the Gender Identity Law took effect through 2025, and regional reporting on 11 July 2026 profiles two historic rectification cases in Ñuble as the region's landmark instances.
tangentialFactors:
Movilh Chile's annual human-rights report, published 18 March 2025 using 2024 data, records 2,847 documented homo/transphobic abuses nationwide, a 78.7% year-on-year rise accounting for 23.5% of all cases since the series began. The report frames this as the first retrogression since the recovery of democracy. Ñuble tops the regional rise table at +300%, the sharpest percentage increase of any Chilean region, though the increase comes off a 1.44% share of the national total.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, recommending elimination of the Gender Identity Support Program, restriction of minors' progressive autonomy, a ban on hormonal treatment for minors and repeal of the circular protecting gender identity in schools. The report does not have the force of law.

The health authorities have issued competing guidance. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, while the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. The Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law on 9 January 2025; that section had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.
localsOnly:
Residents access gender-affirming care through the public health system, which has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013. A 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name.

In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres. The Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

People aged 14 to 18 seeking legal recognition of gender identity apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents; adults apply directly to the Civil Registry. The two rectification cases reported in Ñuble on 11 July 2026 are described as historic for the region, indicating that formal use of the law among Ñuble residents remains limited.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Movilh figure of 2,847 abuses combines homo- and transphobic cases; the inventory does not disaggregate how many involve trans victims, and no case-level detail for Ñuble is sourced. The region's +300% rise is stated against a 1.44% share of the national total, so absolute case numbers in Ñuble are not established here.

The 9 April 2025 Constitutional Court ruling on the under-14 wording applies only to the case before it; how the Gender Identity Law is being applied to under-14 applicants in Ñuble generally is unresolved in the sources.

Whether the Gendarmería de Chile protocol has been implemented in the region's own detention facilities, and how entry examinations and trans-visitor access rules operate there, is not sourced.

Regional reporting characterising the two Ñuble rectification cases as evidence of minimal formal trans presence is a publication's framing rather than an administrative count of trans residents in the region.
